newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Chernomyrdin, Chubais savour victory.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Chernomyrdin, Chubais savour victory.

text.p: Two men in the Kremlin had reason to uncork the champagne on Friday after President Boris Yeltsin's sacking of Alexander Lebed as his security chief.

For Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, the sacking removed a likely presidential rival from public office. For top Kremlin aide Anatoly Chubais, Lebed's dismissal was the result of what many political commentators said was his careful plotting.
Their victory may be short-lived or purely tactical because Lebed could pose just as potent a threat from the ranks of the opposition and still has his sights set on the presidency.
But the glint in Chernomyrdin's eye after Thursday's sacking was a sign of satisfaction with at least a partial victory.
"It was right. It should have been done long ago. Everyone understands this," Chernomyrdin told reporters.
Chubais, the head of the Kremlin administration and often portrayed as its grey cardinal, kept a low profile.
But Lebed pointed an accusing finger at him during a news after his dismissal, saying: "I was an obstacle to plans by Chubais to set up a regency. He wants to become president."
Depicting himself as the victim of a concerted campaign, he said: "I was a black sheep in the flock. It was only a matter of time before they sacked me. I am not part of their flock."

Many politicians said Lebed's departure was just a matter of time after Yeltsin brought him into his team last June following the 46-year-old reserve general's surprisingly strong third place in the first round of a presidential election.
Although Yeltsin regarded Lebed as a counterweight to other forces in the Kremlin, he also set him on collision course with Chubais and Chernomyrdin.
Rivalry with Chernomyrdin was inevitable because both are likely to run in the next presidential election, due in 2000 but possible earlier if the ailing Yeltsin has to step down.
Chernomyrdin, 58, avoided confrontation with Lebed in public but was quick to rebuff the security chief's efforts to have a say in economic matters.
Lebed overshadowed Chernomyrdin in Moscow's efforts to end fighting with separatist rebels in Chechnya and then stole the limelight by signing a peace deal on August 31.
Lebed's independent manoeuvring in almost everything he did in the Kremlin and what seemed his constant meddling undermined Chernomyrdin's authority.

Chubais, 41, was also threatened by Lebed. The former privatisation guru is an unlikely presidential candidate, at least for some years, but Lebed's rise was a threat to his ambitions, which are tied for now to Chernomyrdin and Yeltsin.
Many independent political analysts also say Chubais was the central figure plotting behind the scenes to remove Lebed.

"The behind-the-scenes relations between them (Lebed and Chernomyrdin) are increasingly acquiring the nature of war - brutal and merciless," the influential Argumenty i Fakty weekly newspaper wrote before Lebed's sacking.
"It is probably initiated by Anatoly Chubais. He could not sit back calmly and watch how Lebed was gaining political points and how the latter's popularity had increased."
Many newspapers suggested Chubais, who helped steer Yeltsin to re-election in July, was also behind a media campaign against Lebed which had gathered steam over the last two weeks.

They say he also encouraged a number of ex-Kremlin officials to trade insults in public, partly to attack former Yeltsin security chief Alexander Korzhakov as he tried to form a potentially dangerous alliance with Lebed.

Outside the Kremlin, there was also reason to celebrate at least temporarily in the offices of powerful financial groups and banks, some of which own influential media and back Chubais and Chernomyrdin over the unpredictable Lebed.

The Kremlin and media campaigns against Lebed look set to continue apace as the former security chief joins the opposition, but at the risk of boosting their foe's popularity by making him a victim in the eyes of voters.
